\title{Diagnose, Fix, Measure: An Applied Study of a Database-and-Documents Assistant, and Where a Cheap
Decision Model Can Replace LLM Calls}

\titlerunning{Diagnose, Fix, Measure: a Database-and-Documents Assistant}
\author{Author names (placeholder)}
\authorrunning{Authors (placeholder)}
\institute{Affiliation (placeholder) \\ \email{email (placeholder)}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We report an applied study of StateSync, an assistant that answers questions from a company's SQL database, its
uploaded filings, or both. On FinanceBench's open sample the shipped system answered \N{fbShip} of
\N{fbN} questions correctly. A diagnosis traced most failures to two design flaws: a router that saw only the 20
most recent document titles and nothing of the database, and an answer writer that read the first 8 of 25
retrieved passages in document order. Fixing the design flaws raised accuracy on this development set to
\N{fbBge}, and on a held-out
routing test a single front-door LLM call routed \N{rtLLMAcc} of questions correctly against \N{rtShipAcc} for the shipped
router. For SQL answers, falling back to a pool of candidates when a small trained verifier doubts the first
answer raised execution accuracy on \N{sN} held-out BIRD questions from \N{sFirst} to \N{sPsix}
(pre-registered, \N{sH3P}). Across both parts we test a hosted decision model, Jev, as a cheap replacement for LLM
calls. Used zero-shot it detects wrong SQL answers nearly as well as an LLM judge (AUROC \N{sAurocJev} vs
\N{sAurocJudge}). Asked one choice question, it routes about as accurately as the LLM front door (\N{rtJevCAcc} vs \N{rtLLMrawAcc},
no significant difference) with no LLM call. In a
pre-registered test on \N{pgN} held-out questions it puts the right filing page first \N{pgJBFirst} of the time,
against \N{pgBFirst} for a cross-encoder re-ranker. Used as independent yes/no
decisions, it cannot express that a question needs both sources. We report the negative results alongside the
positive ones.

\keywords{Text-to-SQL \and Retrieval-augmented generation \and Query routing \and Verification \and
Decision models \and Evaluation}
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Assistants that answer business questions increasingly sit in front of two kinds of source at once: a
database of figures and a library of documents. Such a system has to decide where a question should go, find
the right passage or write the right query, and know when its own answer is likely wrong. Each of these
decisions is usually made by another large language model (LLM) call. Each call adds seconds and cost, and
each can fail in its own way.

This paper reports what happened when we measured one such system, StateSync, honestly rather than on the
questions it was built around. The shipped system answered \N{fbShip} of FinanceBench's open questions
\cite{islam2023financebench} correctly. We traced the failures to concrete design flaws, fixed them, and
measured every fix against a baseline. Where we had used a question set to find a flaw, we built a fresh,
held-out set to confirm the fix, and fixed its analysis plan before any data existed. Throughout, we ask
one further question: which of the system's LLM calls can a cheap decision model replace? We use Jev
\cite{typesafe2026jev}, which answers typed yes/no and choice questions about a given state with
probabilities, writes no text, and costs a fraction of a cent per call.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{A diagnosis and its fixes.} We show how a blind router and a passage-ordering choice cost most of
a document assistant's accuracy, and how fixing them raises FinanceBench accuracy from \N{fbShip} to
\N{fbBge}. A single front-door call replaces three LLM calls before routing.
\item \textbf{Detect-then-fallback for SQL.} On \N{sN} held-out BIRD questions \cite{li2023bird}, a trained
verifier's doubt about the first answer triggers a fallback to a pool of 21 candidate queries, raising
execution accuracy from \N{sFirst} to \N{sPsix} (pre-registered, confirmed after Holm correction). Two other pre-registered hypotheses were not confirmed.
\item \textbf{A decision model as a cheap layer.} Jev replaces an LLM judge for flagging wrong SQL answers at
some loss (AUROC \N{sAurocJev} vs \N{sAurocJudge}). Asked one choice question, it replaces the LLM router
(\N{rtJevCAcc} vs \N{rtLLMrawAcc}, no significant difference). In a pre-registered held-out test it moves the right
page to the top of the retrieved passages \N{pgJBFirst} vs \N{pgBFirst} of the time. It fails when its decisions
are posed as independent yes/no questions.
\item \textbf{Negative results, reported.} A ``not answerable'' reply for SQL missed its pre-set bar for false
refusals. The fixed system did not significantly beat the shipped one on held-out two-source questions. A
conformal ``verified'' label never reached usable coverage.
\end{itemize}

\section{System}\label{sec:system}
StateSync answers a question from a connected SQL database, from a workspace's uploaded documents, or from
both. A question takes one of four routes: \emph{sql}, \emph{docs}, \emph{hybrid} (both sources) or
\emph{neither} (a polite refusal).

\paragraph{Shipped pipeline.} Before any answer work, the shipped system made up to three LLM calls: a
normaliser (meant for Hindi and Hinglish questions, which on English passes the text through), a follow-up
rewriter on every turn after the first, and a router. The router saw the question and the titles of the 20
most recently uploaded documents. It saw nothing of the database, and no document beyond those 20.

\paragraph{SQL route.} An LLM agent reads the schema, writes a query, runs it read-only, and on an error or an
empty result reads a remediation hint and retries (at most three times). Its first answer is what Part~S
(Sect.~\ref{sec:sql}) tries to detect as wrong.

\paragraph{Documents route.} A two-round dense search (\texttt{mxbai-embed-large}) first finds the most relevant
documents, then returns up to 25 passages from them. An optional cross-encoder (\texttt{bge-reranker-v2-m3}
\cite{chen2024bgem3}, on the host GPU) re-scores them. The answer writer reads the first 8 of the 25. The
shipped system ordered those 8 by document and by position in the document, not by relevance.

\paragraph{Hybrid route.} The question is split by an LLM into a database part and a documents part. The
shipped split recognised only the identifiers of the product's original e-commerce domain.

\paragraph{Fixed design.} The fixes (Sect.~\ref{sec:docs}) replace the three pre-routing calls with one
\emph{front door}. It is given the question, the last three turns, a \emph{database card} (the dataset's tables
and columns, cached) and the five best-matching documents from one dense search. It returns, as JSON, the
standalone question, whether answering needs the database and the documents (yes, no or unsure each), whether
the question is out of scope, and, when both sources are needed, the split. A fixed table maps the two
needs to a route, so nothing defaults silently to SQL. The writer reads passages in relevance order, with each
passage's filing title and page. The re-ranker also reads the title. For hybrid questions whose documents part
depends on the database part (``which of these companies had the highest revenue, and what does its annual
report say about risks?''), the documents search is narrowed to the filings whose titles name the entities the
SQL result returned.

\paragraph{Jev.} Jev \cite{typesafe2026jev} is a hosted decision model. A request carries a state (any text) and typed
questions: \emph{noul} (is this statement true? answered with a probability) or \emph{choice} (pick one of
named options, with a probability each). It writes no text. We call \texttt{jev-1.13} through OpenCode Zen at
\$0.042 per million input tokens. Sect.~\ref{sec:jev} uses it in five places.

\section{Method}\label{sec:method}
\paragraph{Development and held-out data.} We distinguish data we used to find problems from data we used to
confirm fixes. FinanceBench's open sample \cite{islam2023financebench} (150 questions over 84 SEC filings,
44,918 passages) is our \emph{development} set for the documents route: we diagnosed and fixed the system on
it, so its numbers are not confirmatory. Confirmation comes from four sets built or fixed before their runs:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{BIRD held-out} \cite{li2023bird}: \N{sN} questions of the Mini-Dev set, held out from all
development, scored against corrected gold queries \cite{jin2026annotation}, for the SQL route.
\item \textbf{Routing set}: 224 questions and 24 short conversations over a database of SEC-reported figures for
31 companies and the same 84 filings, labelled \emph{sql}, \emph{docs}, \emph{hybrid}, \emph{either} (both
sources can answer) or \emph{neither}, split into development and test halves before any run. All
prompt and threshold choices were made on the development half; we report the test half
(\N{rtN} questions, \N{rtTurnsN} conversation turns).
\item \textbf{Held-out hybrid set}: 100 two-source questions generated from templates with a fixed seed after
the hybrid design was settled, 60 of them ``dependent'' (the documents part needs the database answer).
\item \textbf{Held-out page set}: \N{pgN} questions written by an LLM (Gemini) from randomly sampled filing
pages, FinanceBench's evidence pages excluded; the gold page is the source page.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Pre-registration.} For Part~S, the hybrid set and the page-finding test, the hypotheses, measures,
tests and thresholds were committed to the repository before the data they test existed or were scored, with a
change log for anything altered later. Analyses decided after seeing results are labelled exploratory.

\paragraph{Grading.} SQL answers are scored by execution against the corrected gold under a relaxed row
comparison. Document answers are graded by an LLM grader (Gemini 3.8 Flash) against FinanceBench's answer and
justification, with a fixed prompt, in one shuffled order, blind to the configuration: correct, partly correct,
incorrect or refused. The primary label is \emph{correct}. A blind second-model check of a random sample of grades is
reported in Sect.~\ref{sec:threats}.

\paragraph{Statistics.} Paired comparisons use the exact McNemar test (sign-flip permutation tests where
outcomes are fractional, as when ties between candidates are scored at their expected accuracy), intervals
from a bootstrap stratified by database (2,000 resamples), and Holm correction within each family of
pre-registered hypotheses.

\paragraph{Run safeguards.} Every comparison runs the product's own code from images built from a recorded
commit, in containers separate from the shared deployment. The harnesses refuse to run on a container whose
image differs from the recorded build, and stop when the front door reports that the database card is missing.
That guard was added after a Docker restart left the SEC database stopped and silently invalidated an afternoon
of routing runs. Those runs were discarded and repeated (Sect.~\ref{sec:threats}).

\section{SQL answers: detect, then fall back}\label{sec:sql}
\paragraph{Pool.} For each of the \N{sN} held-out questions we pooled 21 candidate queries: the pipeline answer of
GPT-5 mini and five self-consistency samples, the same six from gpt-oss-120b, and three standalone samples each
from three further models. Candidates whose results agree form a cluster. The pipeline's own answer, GPT-5 mini's
first candidate, is the \emph{first answer} (\N{sFirst} correct). At least one candidate is right for \N{sOracle}
of questions, which bounds what any selection can reach.

\paragraph{Checkers.} We compare five ways of scoring a candidate. (i)~A ModernBERT-base classifier
\cite{warner2024modernbert}, fine-tuned on execution-labelled candidates from other questions (``real''), or on
the reference query and rule-based mutants of it (``mutation''). (ii)~Laya, a small decision model, zero-shot and
fine-tuned. (iii)~An LLM judge (Gemini 3.8 Flash) giving a 0--100 score. (iv)~Jev, zero-shot, asked ``Does this SQL
query and its result correctly answer the question?''. All see the question, the query and a preview of its
result. Trained checkers are trained, calibrated and tested on rotating folds stratified by database: each question
is scored once, by a model that saw neither it nor its threshold's calibration fold.

\paragraph{Pre-registered hypotheses.} H1: selecting the pool's candidate with the highest ModernBERT score beats a
majority vote. H2: training on real candidates beats training on mutants. H3: a cascade that keeps the first
answer unless ModernBERT doubts it, and then selects from the pool, beats the first answer. The doubt threshold is
fitted per round on the calibration fold.

policies. Pre-registered comparisons are one-sided, Holm-corrected; ``n.s.'' = not significant after correction.}
\label{tab:sql}
\begin{tabular}{lrl}
\toprule
Policy & Accuracy & vs.\ reference \\
\midrule

ModernBERT-max, mutation (H2) & \N{sPfivem} & real vs mutation \N{sH2P}, n.s. \\
\textbf{ModernBERT-triggered cascade (H3)} & \textbf{\N{sPsix}} & +\N{sH3W}/$-$\N{sH3L}, \N{sH3P} \\
ModernBERT score + vote & \N{sPfivev} & exploratory \\
Judge-max & \N{sJudgeMax} & -- \\
Judge-triggered cascade & \N{sJudgeCascade} & -- \\
Laya-max (fine-tuned / zero-shot) & \N{sLayaMax} / \N{sLayaZSMax} & -- \\

\paragraph{Results.} Table~\ref{tab:sql}. H3 is confirmed: the cascade raises accuracy from \N{sFirst} to
\N{sPsix} (paired difference \N{sPsixCI} points, 95\% interval), falling back on \N{sPsixFall} of questions. H1 and
H2 point the expected way but do not survive Holm correction. The best policy we found adds ModernBERT's scores
within each cluster of agreeing candidates (\N{sPfivev}). We found it after the pre-registered analysis, so we
report it as exploratory. Cheaper fallbacks that a product would try first help little: when the judge
doubts the first answer (\N{sJudgeDoubts} of questions), re-voting among GPT-5 mini's own samples reaches
\N{sReVote}, and escalating to gpt-oss's answer \N{sEscalate}.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Detecting a wrong first answer (AUROC, higher is better) and what each checker costs.}
\label{tab:detect}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Checker & AUROC & Training / cost \\
\midrule
LLM judge (Gemini 3.8 Flash) & \N{sAurocJudge} & none; an LLM call per cluster \\
Jev, zero-shot & \N{sAurocJev} & none; \N{sJevCost} for all 6,056 distinct candidates \\
ModernBERT, real & \N{sAurocMB} & 5-fold fine-tuning \\

\paragraph{Detection.} Table~\ref{tab:detect}. The judge detects wrong first answers best. Jev, with no training and
no prompt engineering, comes second, ahead of the trained ModernBERT. The judge's lead over Jev and Jev's lead over
ModernBERT both have bootstrap intervals that include zero. Jev's scores are stable: rescoring 200 candidates gave a
rank correlation of \N{sJevRetest}. Jev is a weak \emph{selector}, though. Picking the candidate it scores highest
gives \N{sJevMax}, little above the first answer.

\paragraph{Jev as the trigger (exploratory).} Because Jev is good at doubting and poor at choosing, we tried it as
the cascade's trigger with ModernBERT-plus-vote as the selector. With Jev's untuned rule ``fall back when
P(correct)~$<0.5$'', accuracy rises to \N{sJthree} (\N{sJthreeP}) while falling back on only \N{sJthreeFall} of
questions. With the threshold fitted like H3's, it reaches \N{sJtwo}. These analyses were decided after the
pre-registered ones and are reported as exploratory.

\paragraph{Approved examples.} A cheaper lever than any checker is to show the SQL writer approved question--query
pairs from the same database (from the training folds). We measured it with gpt-oss-120b and the standalone prompt,
three samples per question per arm. With the product's similarity threshold (E1), only 54 of the \N{sN} questions
get any example, and accuracy moves from \N{sExE0} to \N{sExE1} (\N{sExOneDiff} points, 95\% interval
\N{sExOneCI}). With the three most similar examples and no threshold (E2) it reaches \N{sExE2} (\N{sExTwoDiff},
\N{sExTwoCI}). These gains are measured on a different writer than the cascade's, so they are not directly
comparable to Table~\ref{tab:sql}. But they suggest that labelled questions are worth more as examples than as
verifier training data.

\section{Documents and routing}\label{sec:docs}
\paragraph{Diagnosis.} On FinanceBench the shipped system answered \N{fbShip} of questions correctly and declined
\N{fbShipRefused} of \N{fbN}. Two flaws explain most of it. First, the router sent \N{fbShipToSql} of the \N{fbN}
document questions to SQL: it saw only the 20 newest of 84 titles and nothing of the database, so a question about
a filing outside those 20 looked like a database question. Second, of the \N{fbShipReached} questions that did reach
the documents, only \N{fbShipReachedCorrect} were answered correctly. The search often found the right page, but
the writer read the first 8 of 25 passages \emph{in document order}. The right page was among the 25 for
\N{wwDocAny} of questions but among the writer's 8 for only \N{wwDoc}.

\paragraph{Fixes and their effect (development set).} Ordering the writer's passages by relevance raised the share
of questions whose right page reaches the writer from \N{wwDoc} to \N{wwRel}. Adding the re-ranker, and letting it
read each passage's title, raised it to \N{wwBgeT}. With the front door in place of the router and these
fixes, the system answers \N{fbDense} of FinanceBench correctly without the re-ranker and \N{fbBge} with it,
against \N{fbShip} shipped (+\N{fbBgeW}/$-$\N{fbBgeL}, \N{fbBgeP}). These are development-set numbers. The
held-out tests below and in Sect.~\ref{sec:jev} are the confirmatory evidence.

\paragraph{Routing (held-out test).} Table~\ref{tab:routing} compares routers on the routing set's test half. Here
earlier turns are given as the user typed them, as a system that rewrites nothing would see them. The front door
routes \N{rtLLMrawAcc} of questions correctly against \N{rtShipAcc} for the shipped router
(+\N{rtLLMrawvShipW}/$-$\N{rtLLMrawvShipL}, \N{rtLLMrawvShipP}). With gold rewritten history it reaches
\N{rtLLMAcc}. It gets most two-source questions right (\N{rtLLMrawHybrid}), and it is the only LLM router that
declines out-of-scope questions at all (\N{rtLLMrawNeither}, against \N{rtShipNeither}). A semantic router
(majority label of the five most similar labelled development questions) is a strong cheap baseline at
\N{rtSemAcc}, but it misses most two-source (\N{rtSemHybrid}) and out-of-scope (\N{rtSemNeither}) questions.

\paragraph{Two-source questions (held-out).} On 100 held-out hybrid questions, an answer counts when its database part
is right and it cites the right filing. The shipped system gets \N{hyShip}, the fixed system \N{hyVthree} and the
fixed system with entity narrowing \N{hyEnt}. The pre-registered primary comparison, fixed vs shipped, is
\emph{not} significant (+\N{hyMainW}/$-$\N{hyMainL}, \N{hyMainP}). The pre-registered secondary one is significant:
on the 60 dependent questions, entity narrowing lifts both-parts-right from \N{hyVthreeDep} to \N{hyEntDep}
(+\N{hyEntW}/$-$\N{hyEntL}, \N{hyEntP}). Two weaknesses cap all arms. The front door sent \N{hyVthreeToSql} of the
60 dependent questions to SQL alone. And the database part was right for only \N{hyDbRight} of 100.

\paragraph{Follow-up questions without an extra LLM call.} The shipped system rewrites every follow-up with an LLM.
We replace this with rules. A follow-up is detected by anaphora (``it'', ``its'', ``what about'') or a missing
company. The last company and year mentioned, in the previous answer first, are carried forward. The models that
write the SQL and the answer get one line of context. On the routing set's follow-up turns the rules detect
\N{ccDetected} follow-ups with no false alarm and recover company and year correctly for \N{ccBoth}. Answered end to
end (\N{tuN} turns with gold answers; Jev with the first choice wording), Jev routing plus carry-over gets \N{tuCarry} right with no extra LLM call. That
is against \N{tuNoCtx} without context (+\N{tuCarryNoW}/$-$\N{tuCarryNoL}, \N{tuCarryNoP}), \N{tuShip} for the
shipped LLM rewriter, and \N{tuLLM} for the LLM front door (+\N{tuCarryLLMW}/$-$\N{tuCarryLLML}, \N{tuCarryLLMP}).

\paragraph{A fix that did not ship.} We let the SQL writer reply ``not answerable'' instead of forcing a query. It
had to keep false refusals on 150 answerable held-out BIRD questions at or below 1\%, and three versions missed
(best \N{gFalseNA}). Accuracy was unchanged within run-to-run variation: one configuration run twice gave
\N{gNoiseA} and \N{gNoiseB}. The feature is off in every result above.

\section{Jev as a cheap decision layer}\label{sec:jev}
Across the system, several LLM calls only \emph{decide} something: is this answer wrong, which source is needed,
which passage holds the answer, does this database hold the data. We asked whether a decision model that writes no
text can take these over. Table~\ref{tab:jev} summarises the five uses.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Jev (\texttt{jev-1.13}, zero-shot) in five roles. ``Held-out'' marks results on data that played no part in
the design; ``dev'' marks development-set or exploratory results.}
\label{tab:jev}
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\begin{tabular}{p{3.0cm}p{4.9cm}l}
\toprule
Role & Result & Evidence \\
\midrule
Page finder & right page first \N{pgJBFirst} vs \N{pgBFirst} (bge + titles), +\N{pgPoneW}/$-$\N{pgPoneL}, \N{pgPoneP} & held-out, pre-registered \\
Router (one choice) & \N{rtJevCAcc} vs \N{rtLLMrawAcc} for the LLM front door, \N{rtJevCvLLMP}; no LLM call & held-out \\
Not-answerable gate & AUROC \N{naAuroc}; \N{naFalse} false refusals, \N{naCaught} unanswerable caught & held-out half, easy negatives \\
SQL answer checker & AUROC \N{sAurocJev} vs \N{sAurocJudge} (LLM judge) & held-out \\
SQL retry trigger & \N{sJthree} vs \N{sFirst}, falling back on \N{sJthreeFall} & held-out, exploratory \\
Router (yes/no questions) & \N{rtJevYNAcc}; hybrid \N{rtJevYNHybrid} & held-out (fails) \\
Document answer checker & AUROC \N{dcAuroc} & dev (weak) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Page finding: a pre-registered test.} On FinanceBench, re-ordering the 25 retrieved passages by Jev's
answer to ``Does this passage contain the information needed to answer the question?'' looked promising. But
FinanceBench is our development set, so we pre-registered a confirmatory test. We fixed the seed, the filters, the
question-writer and checker prompts, the arms, the measures and the tests in the repository before the set existed.
The set has \N{pgN} questions, written by Gemini from randomly sampled filing pages; FinanceBench's evidence pages
and their neighbours are excluded. All arms re-order the same 25 passages, so only the order differs. The primary
hypothesis held: Jev puts the right page first \N{pgJBFirst} of the time against \N{pgBFirst} for the re-ranker
(+\N{pgPoneW}/$-$\N{pgPoneL}, \N{pgPoneP}). Without the GPU re-ranker, over dense results alone, Jev reaches
\N{pgJDFirst}. Jev did not improve whether the right page is among the writer's 8 (\N{pgJBWin} vs \N{pgBWin}), which
the re-ranker had already brought close to its ceiling. So the gain is in precision: the first passage, the one a
user is shown as the source, is right four times as often. The cost was \$0.17 for 6,220 passages.

\paragraph{Routing: one choice beats several yes/no questions.} Asked separate yes/no questions (``does answering need
the database?'', ``\ldots the documents?''), Jev routes no better than the shipped router (\N{rtJevYNAcc}). It almost
never chooses both sources (\N{rtJevYNHybrid} hybrid). The reason shows in its probabilities. On development
questions, a question that needs both sources and one that either source can answer get nearly the same scores on
both questions, so no pair of thresholds separates them. Asked one choice question (database only, documents only,
both, or neither), Jev weighs the sources against each other. It gets every hybrid question right (\N{rtJevCHybrid}),
routes \N{rtJevCAcc} overall, not significantly different from the LLM front door (\N{rtJevCvLLMP}), and needs no
LLM call and a median \N{rtJevCMs}\,s instead of \N{rtLLMrawMs}\,s. One description of the options was chosen on the
development half before the single test run. Its weakness is documents-only questions (\N{rtJevCDocs}). It sends some
of them to the database whenever they ask for financial figures, even figures the database does not hold.

\paragraph{A gate for unanswerable SQL questions.} The LLM's ``not answerable'' reply failed its 1\% false-refusal bar
(Sect.~\ref{sec:docs}). We asked Jev ``Does the database described contain the data needed to answer the
question?'' for the 150 held-out BIRD questions, each against its own schema and against a randomly chosen other
database's schema. With the threshold fitted on one half, the other half had \N{naFalse} false refusals while
\N{naCaught} unanswerable pairs were caught. A question asked of the wrong database is an easy negative, so this
shows the gate can meet the bar, not that it would on subtler cases.

\paragraph{Where Jev is weak.} Judging whether a written answer is supported by its cited passages is harder for it. On
the fixed system's FinanceBench answers its AUROC is \N{dcAuroc}, too low to gate answers usefully. And it is a poor
\emph{selector} among SQL candidates, even though it is a good doubter (Sect.~\ref{sec:sql}).

\section{Negative results and threats to validity}\label{sec:threats}
\paragraph{What did not work.} Two of three pre-registered SQL hypotheses (H1, H2) were not confirmed after Holm
correction. A conformal ``verified'' label for SQL answers, meant to mark answers with a guaranteed error rate,
never reached usable coverage at 5\% or 10\%, because the calibration folds were too small for the bound. The
``not answerable'' reply missed its false-refusal bar and was not shipped. On held-out two-source questions the
fixed system did not significantly beat the shipped one. Jev posed as yes/no routing questions failed, and Jev as
a document answer checker was weak.

\paragraph{Development-set numbers.} The FinanceBench gains (\N{fbShip} to \N{fbBge}) were measured on the questions
we used to diagnose the system and are optimistic. The confirmatory evidence for the documents route is the
held-out routing, hybrid and page-finding results.

\paragraph{Generated questions.} The held-out hybrid and page sets were generated, from templates and by an LLM.
Generated questions may be cleaner than users' questions. For pages, another page may also answer a question, which
lowers every arm's measured page accuracy alike. The LLM that wrote page questions (Gemini) also grades document
answers; it never ranks passages.

\paragraph{Graders.} Document answers are graded by an LLM. As a check, a second model (\textbf{[model name]}), blind
to the grader's verdicts and to which configuration produced each answer, graded a random sample of 30 answers. It
agreed with the grader on 27 of 30 (29 of 30 on correct vs.\ not correct). All three disagreements were between
\emph{partly correct} and an adjacent label. This is a check between models, not a human check, and we report it as
such. SQL answers are scored by execution, not by a grader.

\paragraph{A discarded afternoon of runs.} A Docker restart left the SEC database stopped. For several hours, every
front door decided without the database card. We found it when SQL answers failed, discarded the affected runs
(kept, labelled, in the repository), added a guard that stops any run without the card, and repeated them. Every
routing number in this paper comes from the repeated runs.

\paragraph{Scope.} One product, English questions, US public-company filings and one financial database. Several
models are reached through commercial routers whose upstream providers are not disclosed; the served model name is
recorded per call. Jev is a commercial model whose training data we do not know.

\section{Related work}
\textbf{Verification and selection for text-to-SQL.} LEVER \cite{ni2023lever} re-ranks generated programs with a
verifier that reads execution results. CHASE-SQL \cite{pourreza2025chase} selects among multi-path candidates with a
trained selector, and GradeSQL \cite{tritto2025gradesql} trains outcome reward models that beat majority voting.
Richardson \cite{richardson2026predicts} studies which signals predict correctness. Our cascade uses a verifier only
to decide \emph{when} to fall back, and we find that a zero-shot decision model is a good doubter but a poor selector.
\textbf{Cascades.} FrugalGPT \cite{chen2023frugalgpt} escalates to stronger models when a scorer doubts an answer.
\textbf{Adaptive and corrective retrieval.} Adaptive-RAG \cite{jeong2024adaptiverag} routes by predicted question
complexity, and CRAG \cite{yan2024crag} triggers corrective actions from a retrieval evaluator. \textbf{Routing between
databases and documents.} Rule-driven routing between structured and unstructured sources \cite{bai2025routing}
found them complementary and querying both naively costly, which motivates deciding ``both'' deliberately. Our
front door decides it from evidence about both sources. \textbf{Re-ranking.} Cross-encoders such as the BGE family
\cite{chen2024bgem3} are the standard second stage. Our page-finding result suggests a decision model asked a direct
relevance question is a strong precision re-ranker. We found no published evaluation of Jev on SQL answers,
routing or retrieval.

\section{Conclusion}
Measured honestly, a database-and-documents assistant that looked reasonable lost most of its accuracy to two design
choices: what its router was shown, and how its writer's passages were ordered. Fixing them, and confirming each fix
on data that played no part in finding it, was more valuable than any single model upgrade. Across the system, a
cheap decision model can replace LLM calls that only \emph{decide}. It flags wrong SQL answers nearly as well as an
LLM judge. Asked one choice question, it routes about as accurately as an LLM front door, with no significant difference. It finds the right source page
four times as often as a cross-encoder. It fails where the decision is split into independent questions, or where
it must judge prose against evidence. Code, prompts, pre-registrations and every result file are kept with the project's
code (availability: \textbf{to be decided by the authors}).
